question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
Many people love to visit enchanting hills.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. alluring.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "enchanting" means extremely attractive, charming, or delightful; casting a magical spell over someone. (मनमोहक/आकर्षक)
◦ Example: The enchanting view from the hilltop left the tourists speechless.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "alluring", which also means attractive or tempting in a magical/charming way. (लुभावना)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "cool" — means pleasantly low in temperature or calm in manner; it has no connotation of charm or magic, so it does not match "enchanting".

• Option 3: "risky" — means dangerous or involving a chance of harm; this is unrelated to, and almost opposite in feel to, "enchanting".

• Option 4: "echoing" — means producing or repeating a sound (an echo); it describes sound, not charm, so it is unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "enchanting" frequently asked in SSC exams: captivating, bewitching, fascinating, mesmerizing, and spellbinding.

• Do not confuse "enchanting" (attractive/charming) with "enchanted" (put under a magic spell) — both come from the verb "enchant" but are used differently.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word in brackets to fill in the blank.
She has _______ (witty) remarks about everything.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. unamusing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word given in brackets is "witty", which means showing quick and inventive verbal humour; clever and amusing in speech. (हाज़िरजवाब/विनोदी)

• Since the question asks for the ANTONYM of "witty", we need a word that means dull, humourless, or not funny.

• "Unamusing" means not funny or entertaining, which is the direct opposite of "witty". (नीरस/हास्यरहित)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "sorry" — means feeling regret or sadness; it does not relate to humour, so it cannot be an antonym of "witty".

• Option 2: "whimsical" — means playfully quaint or fanciful; this is actually close in meaning to "witty" (a synonym-like word), not its opposite.

• Option 4: "woeful" — means full of sorrow or very bad in quality; it relates to sadness/poor quality, not lack of humour, so it does not fit as precisely as "unamusing".

NOTE

• Other antonyms of "witty" that SSC frequently tests: dull, boring, humourless, dreary, and unfunny.

• Synonyms of "witty" to remember: clever, humorous, sharp, quick-witted, and droll.

question: Select the sentence that does NOT have a spelling error.
option_1: The paintings are structured chronologically, starting from cubism to surealism.
option_2: The artist received recognition for her impressive etchings, buclic landscapes, and recreation of natural scenes around her.
option_3: The insouciance of the rock star considering the importance of the occasion, came as a shock to the audience who expected stressful moments.
option_4: The focus of the exibition is to reinforce versatility and creative thinking.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The insouciance of the rock star considering the importance of the occasion, came as a shock to the audience who expected stressful moments.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Option 3 is the only sentence in which every word is spelt correctly, including the difficult word "insouciance" (a feeling of casual unconcern or carefree indifference).

• All the other three options contain a misspelt word, as shown below.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "surealism" is misspelt; the correct spelling is "surrealism" (double "r").

• Option 2 is incorrect because "buclic" is misspelt; the correct spelling is "bucolic" (relating to pleasant rural life).

• Option 4 is incorrect because "exibition" is misspelt; the correct spelling is "exhibition" (with an "h" after "ex").

NOTE

• Commonly misspelt SSC words to remember: surrealism, bucolic, exhibition, insouciance, chronologically, questionnaire, and connoisseur.

• When checking spelling questions, pay special attention to silent letters (like the "h" in "exhibition") and doubled consonants (like the "rr" in "surrealism").

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Repulse
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Repel.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Repulse" means to drive back or reject with a show of distaste or force; to repel. (विकर्षित करना/दूर हटाना)
◦ Example: The soldiers managed to repulse the enemy attack.

• Its closest synonym among the options is "Repel", which also means to drive or force back; to cause distaste or aversion. (प्रतिकर्षित करना)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Substitute" — means to replace one thing with another; it has no connection with driving something back.

• Option 3: "Recover" — means to return to a normal state, or to get something back; this is unrelated to "repulse".

• Option 4: "Reprove" — means to scold or express disapproval; while it sounds similar to "repulse", its meaning (to rebuke) is entirely different.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "Repulse" with the similar-sounding "Reprove" (to scold) or "Repose" (to rest) — these are common SSC distractors.

• Other synonyms of "repulse/repel" tested in SSC: rebuff, resist, ward off, and drive back.

question:
The given sentence is divided into four segments. Select the option that has the segment with a grammatical error.
The employees were comfortable / with me and they talked about / their problems since / I has worked there as a manager.
option_1: I has worked there as a manager.
option_2: with me and they talked about
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. I has worked there as a manager.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "I has worked there as a manager" contains a subject-verb agreement error.

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement: The pronoun "I" always takes the auxiliary verb "have" (not "has"), regardless of tense, in the Present Perfect and related structures.
◦ Correct: I have worked, not I has worked.

• Since the pronoun "I" is used, the correct form must be "I have worked there as a manager."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 ("with me and they talked about") is correct as it stands and contains no grammatical error.

• Option 3 ("their problems since") is correct as it stands and contains no grammatical error.

• Option 4 ("The employees were comfortable") is correct as it stands — "employees" being plural correctly takes "were".

NOTE

• Remember: "has" is used with third-person singular subjects (he, she, it, and singular nouns), while "have" is used with I, we, you, they, and plural nouns.

• This is one of the most frequently tested SSC error-spotting patterns — always check subject-verb agreement first when a sentence contains "has/have/is/are/was/were".

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Select the option that arranges the parts in the correct sequence to form a meaningful sentence.
(P) the sun
(Q) to our planet, Earth
(O) provides essential energy
(R) sustaining life and warmth
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. POQR.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Arranging the parts logically: (P) the sun is the subject, (O) provides essential energy is the main verb phrase, (Q) to our planet, Earth names the recipient, and (R) sustaining life and warmth is the concluding participial phrase.

• Combining in the order P-O-Q-R gives a complete, meaningful sentence: "The sun provides essential energy to our planet, Earth, sustaining life and warmth."

• Rule: In sentence-arrangement questions, first identify the subject (who/what performs the action), then the verb phrase, then the object/recipient, and place any participial or descriptive phrase at the end.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 (QROP) is incorrect because it begins with "to our planet, Earth", which cannot logically start the sentence without a subject.

• Option 3 (ROQP) is incorrect because it begins with the participial phrase "sustaining life and warmth", which cannot stand as the opening of the sentence.

• Option 4 (ORPQ) is incorrect because it places the verb phrase before the subject, producing an ungrammatical order.

NOTE

• In parts-arrangement (jumbled sentence) questions, always locate the part with the subject/main noun first — it almost always begins the sentence unless the sentence has a fronted adverbial or is a question.

question:
Select the correct option to form a meaningful sentence.
I / that / the chef / to work / in / the new / heard / restaurant / is going / across the road.
(a)   (b)   (c)   (d)   (e)   (f)   (g)   (h)   (i)   (j)
option_1: a, c, g, b, h, i, f, e, d, j
option_2: a, b, d, c, e, f, h, g, i, j
option_3: a, b, d, c, g, e, f, h, i, j
option_4: a, g, b, c, i, d, e, f, h, j
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. a, g, b, c, i, d, e, f, h, j.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The scrambled words are: (a) I, (b) that, (c) the chef, (d) to work, (e) in, (f) the new, (g) heard, (h) restaurant, (i) is going, (j) across the road.

• Arranging them in the order a, g, b, c, i, d, e, f, h, j gives: "I heard that the chef is going to work in the new restaurant across the road."

• Rule: The sentence must follow the structure Subject (I) + Verb (heard) + Object clause introduced by "that" (that the chef is going to work in the new restaurant across the road), with the prepositional phrases "in the new restaurant" and "across the road" placed in their natural, logical positions.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (a, c, g, b, h, i, f, e, d, j) is incorrect because it produces the meaningless order "I the chef heard that restaurant is going the new in to work across the road."

• Option 2 (a, b, d, c, e, f, h, g, i, j) is incorrect because it places "that to work the chef" together, which is grammatically broken.

• Option 3 (a, b, d, c, g, e, f, h, i, j) is incorrect for the same reason — it separates "the chef" from its verb "is going" and disrupts the clause structure.

NOTE

• In such multi-part rearrangement questions, first find the main subject and verb of the sentence (here "I heard"), then identify the noun clause introduced by "that", and finally place the descriptive phrases in a logical sequence.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the word in brackets to fill in the blank.
Listening to the same lecture everyday appeared very ___________ to him. (boring)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. monotonous.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word given in brackets is "boring", meaning dull, tedious, and uninteresting, especially due to repetition.

• "Monotonous" means lacking variety and repetitive to the point of being dull or tedious, which closely matches "boring" in this context. (नीरस/एकसुरा)
◦ Example: The monotonous hum of the engine put the passengers to sleep.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "furious" — means extremely angry; this has nothing to do with being repetitive or dull.

• Option 3: "nervous" — means anxious or apprehensive; this does not match the meaning of "boring".

• Option 4: "monolithic" — means large, undifferentiated, and unified as a single block (often used of organizations or structures); despite sounding similar to "monotonous", its meaning is unrelated to "boring".

NOTE

• Do not confuse "monotonous" (repetitive/dull) with the similarly spelt "monolithic" (massive and uniform) — this is a common SSC distractor pair.

• Other synonyms of "boring": tedious, dull, humdrum, tiresome, and wearisome.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
My sisters wished me good luck before I went on the stage to sing.
option_1: Told me to sit on the fence
option_2: Told me to break a leg
option_3: Told me to break the ice
option_4: Told me to break an arm
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Told me to break a leg.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined segment "wished me good luck" needs to be replaced with an option carrying the same meaning.

• The idiom "to break a leg" means to wish someone good luck, especially before a performance. (शुभकामनाएं देना)
◦ Example: Before her final exam, her friends told her to break a leg.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Told me to sit on the fence" — means to remain neutral or undecided on an issue; unrelated to wishing luck.

• Option 3: "Told me to break the ice" — means to initiate conversation in an awkward or formal setting; unrelated to wishing luck.

• Option 4: "Told me to break an arm" — this is not an established idiom and has no meaning of wishing someone luck; it is a deliberate distortion of "break a leg".

NOTE

• Other performance/theatre-related idioms tested in SSC: "steal the show" (to attract the most attention), "bring the house down" (to receive enormous applause), and "in the limelight" (to be the centre of attention).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Five years later, I was eating this same dish at the same restaurant.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. am eating.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence **"Five years later, I ___ this same dish at the same restaurant"** describes a fixed, already-decided plan viewed from the present.

• Rule — Present Continuous for a definite future plan: The Present Continuous Tense (Subject + am/is/are + V-ing) is used to express a planned or arranged future action, especially one that is treated as settled.
◦ Example: I am meeting my cousin next month.

• Applying the rule, "am eating" correctly expresses this settled future plan: "Five years later, I am eating this same dish at the same restaurant."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "will have be eating" is incorrect because it is a grammatically malformed structure — the correct Future Perfect Continuous form would be "will have been eating", not "will have be eating".

• Option 2: "has been eating" is incorrect because the Present Perfect Continuous describes an action that started in the past and is still continuing now — it does not fit a reference to a point five years ahead.

• Option 4: "had been eating" is incorrect because the Past Perfect Continuous describes an action that was ongoing before another past action — there is no such past reference point here.

NOTE

• Present Continuous can be used for near-future planned events (I am leaving tomorrow) as well as for actions happening right now — context decides which meaning applies.

• Do not confuse Future Perfect Continuous (will have been + V-ing) with the incorrect form "will have be + V-ing", which is never grammatically valid.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
O. went
P. yesterday
Q. we
R. to the
S. park
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. QORSP.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The scrambled parts are: O. went, P. yesterday, Q. we, R. to the, S. park.

• Arranging them in the order Q-O-R-S-P gives the meaningful sentence: "We went to the park yesterday."

• Rule: A simple past-tense sentence follows the structure Subject + Verb + Object/Place + Time adverb, with the time adverb (here "yesterday") typically placed at the end of the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (RQOSP) is incorrect because it begins with "to the", which cannot start a sentence without a subject.

• Option 2 (OPQRS) is incorrect because it begins with the verb "went" before the subject "we" is introduced, producing an ungrammatical order.

• Option 3 (PSROQ) is incorrect because it begins with "yesterday park", which is not a coherent way to open the sentence.

NOTE

• In sentence-rearrangement questions with time adverbs like "yesterday", "today", or "tomorrow", these words are usually placed either at the very beginning or the very end of the sentence, not in the middle.

question:
Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the given sentence.
One must be confident of winning and gaining one's goals and must face situations, disasters, trials and setbecks of life with confidence.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Setbecks.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "setbacks" — meaning reversals or difficulties that hinder progress — not "setbecks".

• The word is formed from "set" + "back" (a check or reversal in progress), so it must retain the "a" in "back": set-backs.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Trials" is spelt correctly.

• Option 2: "Disasters" is spelt correctly.

• Option 3: "Confident" is spelt correctly.

NOTE

• Other compound words built with "back" that are commonly tested for spelling: backdrop, backlash, backbone, and feedback.

• Always check compound words carefully — SSC frequently swaps a vowel (like "a" to "e") to create a plausible-looking misspelling.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Paralysed
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Healthy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given word is "Paralysed", meaning unable to move or function normally, especially due to injury, illness, or disease affecting the nerves or muscles. (लकवाग्रस्त/निष्क्रिय)

• Its antonym among the options is "Healthy", meaning being in a state of good physical or functional condition; able to function normally. (स्वस्थ)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Demure" — means shy, modest, or reserved in behaviour; this is unrelated to physical function and so cannot be the antonym of "paralysed".

• Option 2: "Stifled" — means suppressed or restrained, which is actually close in meaning to "paralysed" (restricted), not its opposite.

• Option 3: "Sultry" — means hot and humid, or sensually attractive; it has no connection with physical ability or function.

NOTE

• Other antonyms of "paralysed" that SSC may test: active, agile, mobile, and functional.

• Synonyms of "paralysed" to remember: immobilized, incapacitated, disabled, and numb.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
The list of subjects to be discussed at a meeting
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Agenda.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "The list of subjects to be discussed at a meeting" is precisely defined by the one-word substitute "Agenda". (कार्यसूची/एजेंडा)
◦ Example: The chairperson circulated the agenda for tomorrow's meeting.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Minutes" — refers to the official written record of what was discussed and decided during a meeting, not the list of topics to be discussed beforehand.

• Option 2: "Objectives" — refers to the goals or aims of an action or plan, not specifically the list of meeting subjects.

• Option 4: "Menu" — refers to a list of food items available in a restaurant, unrelated to meetings.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "Agenda" (list of topics before a meeting) with "Minutes" (record of what happened during a meeting) — this pair is very frequently tested together in SSC exams.

• Other meeting-related one-word substitutes: "Quorum" (the minimum number of members required to be present) and "Proxy" (a person authorized to act on another's behalf).

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
The drug pedlar was arrested by the narcotics team.
option_1: The narcotics team was arrested the drug pedlar.
option_2: The narcotics team arrest the drug pedlar.
option_3: The narcotics team arrested the drug pedlar.
option_4: The narcotics team has arrested the drug pedlar.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The narcotics team arrested the drug pedlar.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "The drug pedlar was arrested by the narcotics team" is in the Passive Voice, Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "the narcotics team" becomes the subject; the verb "arrested" (V2, past tense) is used directly; and "the drug pedlar" (originally the subject of the passive sentence) becomes the object.
◦ Active: The narcotics team arrested the drug pedlar.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it wrongly retains the passive form "was arrested" in what should be an active-voice sentence, producing an ungrammatical structure.

• Option 2 is incorrect because it uses the wrong tense — "arrest" (simple present) does not match the original Simple Past Tense of the passive sentence.

• Option 4 is incorrect because it uses the Present Perfect Tense ("has arrested"), which does not correspond to the Simple Past Tense used in the given passive sentence.

NOTE

• When converting Passive to Active voice, always match the tense of the original passive verb exactly — only the subject/object positions change, not the tense.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an adverbial usage error.
Mr. Arun / will pay dear / for his / financial mistake.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. will pay dear.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "will pay dear" contains an adverbial usage error — the word "dear" is used here as an adjective, but the sentence requires an adverb to modify the verb "pay".

• Rule: To modify a verb, an adverb must be used, not an adjective. The adverb form of "dear" (in the sense of "at great cost") is "dearly".
◦ Correct: "will pay dearly" — meaning will suffer serious consequences.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 ("Mr. Arun") is correct as it stands — it is simply the subject of the sentence and contains no error.

• Option 3 ("for his") is correct as it stands and contains no grammatical error.

• Option 4 ("financial mistake") is correct as it stands — a noun phrase used correctly as the object of the preposition "for".

NOTE

• Common adjective/adverb confusion pairs tested in SSC: dear/dearly, hard/hardly, late/lately, near/nearly, and high/highly — each pair has a distinct meaning, so an adjective cannot simply substitute for its "-ly" adverb form.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
We have postponed this movie outing too many times, so we are going tomorrow, come _____ or shine.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. rain.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "come rain or shine" means whatever happens; regardless of circumstances or difficulties. (चाहे कुछ भी हो जाए)
◦ Example: He goes for his morning walk, come rain or shine.

• In the given sentence, since the plan has already been postponed too many times, the speaker asserts the outing will happen tomorrow no matter what — which is exactly the sense conveyed by "come rain or shine".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "mountain" — does not form part of any standard idiom with "come ... or shine"; it does not fit the fixed expression.

• Option 3: "hail" — while hail is a weather phenomenon, the fixed idiom specifically uses "rain", not "hail"; "come hail or shine" is not the standard expression.

• Option 4: "thunder" — similarly, this does not fit the fixed idiomatic expression, which specifically pairs "rain" with "shine".

NOTE

• Other idioms using weather-related pairs of opposites: "through thick and thin" (in good times and bad), "for better or for worse", and "come what may" — all mean regardless of circumstances.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
A. needs to be
B. the shelf in
C. a piece of wood
D. the kitchen
E. need to buy
F. replaced, so I will
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. BDAFEC.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The scrambled parts are: A. needs to be, B. the shelf in, C. a piece of wood, D. the kitchen, E. need to buy, F. replaced, so I will.

• Arranging them in the order B-D-A-F-E-C gives the meaningful sentence: "The shelf in the kitchen needs to be replaced, so I will need to buy a piece of wood."

• Rule: The sentence structure requires the subject (the shelf in the kitchen) followed by the main clause verb phrase (needs to be replaced), then the consequence clause introduced by "so" (so I will need to buy a piece of wood).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (BEFCAD) is incorrect because it disrupts the logical clause order, placing "need to buy" before "needs to be replaced", which breaks the cause-effect sequence.

• Option 2 (ACDBFE) is incorrect because it starts with "needs to be", which requires a subject before it and cannot begin the sentence.

• Option 3 (DEBACF) is incorrect because it starts with "the kitchen need to buy", which is not a coherent grammatical unit.

NOTE

• In such rearrangement questions, first identify the complete subject phrase (here "the shelf in the kitchen"), then trace the cause (needs to be replaced) before the effect introduced by "so".

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
Scientists were conducting experiments on the newly discovered species.
option_1: Experiments on the newly discovered species had been conducted by the scientists.
option_2: The newly discovered species has been conducting experiments by scientists.
option_3: The newly discovered species has been experimented on by scientists.
option_4: Experiments were being conducted on the newly discovered species by scientists.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Experiments were being conducted on the newly discovered species by scientists.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "Scientists were conducting experiments on the newly discovered species" is in the Active Voice, Past Continuous Tense.

• Rule — Past Continuous Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + was/were + V-ing + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + being + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "experiments" becomes the subject; since it is plural, the auxiliary is "were"; "being" is added; the verb "conducting" becomes the past participle "conducted"; and "scientists" becomes the agent introduced by "by".
◦ Passive: Experiments were being conducted on the newly discovered species by scientists.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "had been conducted" is the passive form of the Past Perfect Tense, not the Past Continuous Tense.

• Option 2 is incorrect because it wrongly makes "the newly discovered species" the subject performing the action ("has been conducting"), which reverses the actual meaning — the species did not conduct experiments.

• Option 3 is incorrect because it also wrongly treats "the newly discovered species" as the grammatical subject, and uses the Present Perfect Tense, not the Past Continuous Tense.

NOTE

• When converting Active to Passive, always keep the true object of the action (here "experiments", not "the species") as the subject of the passive sentence.

• Passive of Continuous tenses always uses the structure being + V3 — this is a frequently tested pattern in SSC grammar sections.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.
He had ________ the ________ into smaller clips.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. clipped, clipping.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence **"He had ________ the ________ into smaller clips"** requires a past participle verb in the first blank and a noun in the second blank.

• "Clipped" (past participle of the verb "to clip", meaning to cut) correctly completes the Past Perfect structure "He had clipped...".

• "Clipping" here functions as a noun, referring to a piece cut out (e.g. from a newspaper or magazine), which fits as the object being cut into smaller "clips" (pieces).
◦ Complete sentence: "He had clipped the clipping into smaller clips."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 ("clipping, clips") is incorrect because "He had clipping" is not a valid Past Perfect structure — the main verb after "had" must be a past participle ("clipped"), not the "-ing" form.

• Option 2 ("clipping, clipped") is incorrect for the same reason — "had clipping" is grammatically invalid.

• Option 3 ("clips, clipping") is incorrect because "He had clips" does not fit the intended meaning of an action being performed, and "the clipping" (a noun) must come after "the" rather than "clips".

NOTE

• After the auxiliary "had" (Past Perfect Tense), the main verb must always be in its past participle (V3) form.

• The word "clip" can function as a noun (a small piece, or a fastening device) as well as a verb (to cut or fasten) — such dual-function words are commonly tested in SSC fill-in-the-blank questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.

In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

People often say that the stars govern their fate but they forget the fact that success or failure is the result of one's own (1)_________. If we sow chaff, we can't reap grain; and the result or consequence of an action depends on what one does and to the extent he (2)_________ it. If we work hard, we succeed only to the extent that we work. • "Unpunished" correctly completes this parallel structure, meaning that evil deeds always eventually receive punishment.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "vile" is an adjective meaning extremely unpleasant or morally wicked; grammatically it cannot follow "never go" in this structure, and it does not complete the intended parallel meaning.

• Option 4: "waste" does not fit either grammatically or logically — "evil deeds never go waste" does not convey the intended meaning of punishment/consequence.

• The prefix "un-" added to a past participle (e.g., unrewarded, unpunished, unnoticed) creates a common pattern in SSC cloze passages expressing "not receiving X" — recognizing this prefix pattern helps quickly identify the correct option.

• Parallel structures ("never go unrewarded" / "never go unpunished") are a favourite SSC cloze-test device — once you spot the first half of the parallel, the second half's answer often mirrors it in form.
